Surah Al-Insan

It is also called Surat al-Dahr, Surat al-Abrar, Surat al-Amshaj, and Surat Hal Ata. It is Meccan according to the majority, as is reported in al-Bahr. Mujahid and Qatadah said it is entirely Medinan. Al-Hasan, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi said it is Medinan except for one verse, which is Meccan, namely ﴿And do not obey from them any sinner or disbeliever﴾. It was also said that it is Medinan except from His words, exalted is He, ﴿So be patient for the decision of your Lord﴾ [al-Insan: 24] to the end of the surah, for that part is Meccan. Ibn Adil relates that the Medinan character of the surah is stated without qualification, on the authority of the majority, and that the Shi'ah also hold this view. Its verses number thirty-one, without any disagreement. The connection between it and what precedes it is most evident.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ Its original form, as has been said, is "a-hal" (أهل), with the interrogative used for confirmation (taqrir), meaning that the statement that follows the interrogative is to be affirmed. The one being confirmed is the one who denies resurrection, and it is known that they would say "Yes, a period of time has passed over man when he was not like this." It is then said: "So the One who brought him into existence after he was not, how can it be impossible for Him to bring him back to life after his death?" "Hal" may also mean "qad" (indeed), which is used for approximation, that is, bringing the past close to the present. When "hal" took the place of the hamzah, it indicated both its meaning and the meaning of the hamzah together, and then it became a fixed usage for that. Thus it is for confirmation and approximation. In support of this original form, one cites the verse of Zayd al-Khayl:

Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about our strength, "Did they see us at the slope of the level ground with its hills?"

It has also been said that it is purely interrogative, with no approximation. Its combination with the hamzah in the verse is for emphasis, as in the line:

"Nor is there ever a remedy for the one afflicted by it."

Rather, emphasis is closer here, since the two particles are not identical in form. Al-Sirafi said: the correct reading is "am hal ra'una," with "am" being disjunctive, meaning "bal" (rather). Al-Suyuti, in his commentary on the witnesses of al-Mughni, said: what I saw in an old manuscript of the Diwan of Zayd is "fa-hal ra'una" with the fa'. It is related from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah that it here means "qad," and a group of grammarians interpreted it so, such as al-Kisai, Sibawayh, al-Mubarrad and al-Farra', and it was taken to mean approximation. Some people took it to mean certainty. Abu Ubaydah said: its figurative sense is "qad ata 'ala al-insan," and it is not an interrogative; he apparently meant that it is not an interrogative in the strict sense, but is an interrogative of confirmation, and in the end it returns to "qad ata." Probably the intent of those who interpreted it thus, such as Ibn Abbas and others, is what has been mentioned, and not that it means "qad" in the literal sense. In al-Mughni is what you will benefit from if you review it with insight, so review it.

"Man" here refers to the species, as Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas. "Hin" is a bounded portion of time, applicable to both long and short durations. "Dahr" is time extended without limit, and it applies to the entire duration of the world and to any long unspecified period. "Zaman" is general to all of these. "Dahr" as the container of time is a philosophical expression.

Imam Abu Hanifah hesitated concerning the meaning of "dahr" in oaths, namely its customary meaning in oaths, to the point that it is asked: by what does one break an oath if he says, "By Allah, I will not speak to him for a dahr"? For him, the definite form means the lifetime of the one swearing when there is no intention, and likewise according to his two companions. The indefinite form, according to them, is like "hin"; and "hin," whether definite or indefinite, is like "zaman," six months if there is no intention, and also by that which was intended, according to the correct view. As for the widely reported account of differing verdicts of the four Caliphs on this matter during the time of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, each supporting his view with evidence, it is not established.

And the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, after it was attributed to him: "My companions are like the stars; whichever of them you follow, you will be guided."

However, he preferred the verdict of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honor his face, that "hin" is a day and a night, because of the ease it provides. This is not sound, as is not hidden from the discerning critic. And even if it were sound, one would not turn away from the verdict of the Commander, the source of valor and chivalry, after choosing it, the city of knowledge and the pride of prophethood and messengership.

The meaning here is: "Has there come upon" the species of "man," before a recent time, a bounded, determined portion existing within extended time, ﴿when he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾? Indeed he was a thing, but not one worth mentioning as a human being at all; that is, not known by it. The negation applies to the qualifier, and the meaning is that he did not exist in himself. Rather, what existed was his origin, which is not called a human and is not designated by the title of humanity. This is his remote material, namely the elements, or his intermediate material, namely foods, or his proximate material, namely the sperm drawn from foods created from the elements. The clause ﴿he was not﴾ etc. is a circumstantial clause from "man," meaning "not worth mentioning." It is also permitted that it be an attribute of "hin," with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "he was not in it a thing worth mentioning," as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123]. Applying "man" to its material is a figurative usage, by treating what is potential as if it were actual, or it is of the first type of metonymy. It has also been said that "man" here refers to Adam, peace be upon him. The first view is supported by His words, exalted is He,

[Page 152]

﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop﴾. For man contains the knowledge of his return, so the two do not separate. How so? Moreover, placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun carries the virtue of confirmation and establishment in the soul. When the two differ in generality and specificity, the harmony is lost. There is no doubt that interpreting it as referring to Adam, peace be upon him, in this context is baseless, and there is no objection to it from the view that it refers to the genus (jins), on the basis that it has neither generality nor specificity.

Yes, His words, glorified is He, ﴿from a sperm-drop﴾ indicate that the intended meaning is other than Adam, or that it is a case of predominance (taghlib, the use of a term for the majority to include all). It was also said that what belongs to the majority is ascribed to the whole, as a metaphor in the attribution or in the adverbial sense. Its intended meaning (i.e., Adam) is narrated from Qatada, al-Thawri, Ikrima, al-Sha'bi, and also Ibn 'Abbas. In the narration of Abu Salih from him, he said: "Forty years passed over him before the spirit was breathed into him, while he was lying between Makkah and al-Ta'if."

In the narration of al-Dahhak from him: he was created from clay, and he remained for forty years; then from black mud shaped into form (hama' masnun), and he remained for forty years; then from dried clay (salsal), and he remained for forty years. So his creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years, and then the spirit was breathed into him. Al-Mawardi (a classical scholar) related from him that the term "hin" mentioned here is a long, extended period whose duration is not known.

A similar report is narrated from Ikrima. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he said: "Indeed, among 'hin' there is a period that cannot be known," and he recited the verse, then said: "By God, he does not know how much time passed over him until God created him."

I have seen that some Sufis (al-mutasawwifa) held that the interrogative ﴿hal﴾ here is a rhetorical interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), meaning it is in the sense of negation: that there passed over man no period of time in which he was not something mentioned. Its apparent meaning is a claim of the eternity of man in time, in the sense that there has never been a time without a human being in it. This is the specific eternity (al-qidam al-nawi, eternity of the species) as held by some of the philosophers (falasifa), and it is unbelief by consensus (ijma'). It has been given an interpretation: they meant the thingness (shay'iyya) of established reality (thubut) for the eternity of man according to that consideration, not the thingness of existence (wujud), since in relation to existence it is temporally originated. This is pointed to by the words of Shaykh Muhyi al-Din (Ibn al-Arabi) in chapter 358 of the *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya* (The Meccan Openings):

"If there were not in the world one who is in the form of the Real, the aim of knowing the Real would not have been achieved, namely the originated knowledge in His saying, glorified is He:

'I was a hidden treasure, I was not known, so I loved to be known, so I created the creation, and I made Myself known to them, and they knew Me.'"

So he made Himself a treasure, and a treasure is only hidden within something. Thus the treasure of the Real Himself was only in the form of the Perfect Human in the thingness of its established reality. There the Real was hidden. When the Real clothed man in the thingness of existence, the treasure appeared through its manifestation, so the Perfect Human knew it through its existence, and knew that it had been hidden in him in the thingness of its established reality, while he was not aware of it. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that all things in the thingness of established reality are eternal, not man alone. Perhaps they say that man is "everything," because he is the Manifest Imam, and He, glorified is He, has said: ﴿And every thing We have enumerated in a Manifest Imam﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12]. The discussion of this matter is long, and we cannot afford to extend it. Yet we say: that ﴿hal﴾ here is for denial is a denied (munkar) claim, and that the claim of its correctness is one of the great calamities (al-kibar). What the eminent Companions, may God be pleased with them, understood from the verse is an affirmative informative statement (al-ikhbar al-ijabi).

'Abd ibn Humayd and others transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he heard a man reciting ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ and he said: "Would that it were completed!" [i.e., that it were a clear affirmation].

And from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, that he heard a man reciting that and said: "O would that it were completed!" and for this statement he was punished: he took a stick from the ground and said: "O would that I were like this!"

﴿Amshaj﴾ is the plural of mashaj, with two fathas like sabab and asbab, or mashij, with fatha then kasra like katif and aktaf, or masheej like shahid and ashhad, and nasir and ansar; that is, mixtures, the plural of khalt in the sense of mukhtalit (mixed) and mumtazij (blended). It is said: "I mixed the thing (mashajta al-shay') if you mixed and blended it," so it is mashij and mamshuj. It is an adjective of ﴿nutfa﴾ (sperm-drop), and it is described with the plural form although it is singular, because what is meant by it is the combined fluid of the man and the woman. The plural may be used for more than one, or by consideration of the differing parts in them, in thinness and thickness, yellowness and whiteness, nature and strength, weakness, until some of them became specific to some of the organs, according to what God, by His wisdom, willed, and so He created him by His power.

In some reports it is stated: "What is from sinew, bone, and strength is from the man's fluid, and what is from flesh and blood is from the woman's fluid." The conclusion is that the described noun has been treated as occupying the position of the plural, and it was described with the attributes of its parts. It was also said that it is singular but came in the pattern af'al, like a'shar and akyash in their saying "burma a'shar" (a broken cooking pot) and "burd akyash" (a cloth woven twice, i.e., of double-spun yarn).

Al-Zamakhshari (a classical grammarian and exegete) chose this view. The well-known position from the explicit text of Sibawayh (the grammarian) and the majority of grammarians is that af'al cannot be a plural. It is related from him that he went to this view regarding ʿām (year). The meaning of "nutfa mukhtalita" (a mixed sperm-drop) according to most is a sperm-drop in which the two fluids were mixed and blended. It was also said: in it blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile were mixed. It was also said that the amshaj are the very mixtures, which are an expression for these four, so it is as if it were said: from a sperm-drop which is an expression for four mixtures.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "Amshaj" means colors, i.e., having colors, for the man's fluid is white and the woman's is yellow; when they mix and remain in the bottom of the womb, they become green, just as water turns green by stagnation. It is narrated from al-Kalbi. And it was transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam that he said: "The amshaj are the veins that are in the sperm-drop," and this is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, i.e., having veins. It is narrated from Ikrima, and likewise from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "amshaj" means stages (atwar), i.e., having stages, for the sperm-drop becomes a clot ('alaqa), then a lump of flesh (mudgha), and so on until the completion of the creation and the breathing of the spirit.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿nabtalihi﴾ ("that We may test him") is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "khalaqna" (We created). The meaning is: intending to test him and examine him by imposing obligations afterwards, on the basis that the circumstance is a future one (muqaddara); or: transferring him from state to state and from stage to stage, in the manner of metaphor (isti'ara), because what is transferred appears in each appearance as another appearance, like the appearance of the result of trial and examination after it.

A similar view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. On both interpretations, what is said is resolved: that the testing by obligation occurs after his being made ﴿hearing and seeing﴾, not before, so how does His saying, glorified is He, ﴿so We made him hearing and seeing﴾ follow from it? It was also said that the speech is according to inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the sentence is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf ta'lili), meaning: "So We made him hearing and seeing [in order] that We may test him." This was related from al-Farra' (a grammarian), but it is strained, because the inversion does not occur in its proper place, neither verbally, due to the particle fa', nor in meaning, since the question does not arise before the making. The more correct is the first view. This making is like what is caused by the testing, because the purpose of making him thus is that he should look at the signs on the horizons and within himself, and hear the evidences of revelation. For this reason, He joined with fa' the making to the creation which is restricted by it, and made His saying, exalted is He, follow from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾. It is a resumptive (*mustaʾnafa*) clause giving the reason (*taʿlīliyya*), with the sense of "because We guided him." That is, We made him understand, through the transmitted proofs (*al-dalāʾil al-samʿiyya*) that lead him to it, such as the revealed signs (*al-ayat al-tanzīliyya*), and the rational proofs, such as the signs of the horizons and of the self (*al-ayat al-afaqiyya wa'l-anfusiyya*). This guidance occurs only after the imposition of obligation (*al-taklīf*) and trial (*al-ibtilāʾ*). ﴿either grateful or ungrateful﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (*ḥalān*) relating to the object of "guided." The *immā* may be for detailing (*li'l-tafṣīl*), in view of the multiplicity of states while the subject remains one, meaning: We guided him and showed him the way that leads to the goal in both his states, of gratitude and of ingratitude. Or it may be for division (*li'l-taqsīm*) of the guided, according to the differences of their persons and attributes, meaning: We guided him to the way, divided into two kinds of people: some are grateful, by being guided to the truth and its path, by taking up that path; and some are ungrateful, by turning away from it. The sum is: We showed him the guidance and Islam. So among them is the one who is guided and Muslim, and among them is the one who is astray and a disbeliever.

It was also said that they are two circumstantial clauses relating to "the way," meaning: We made the way known to him, as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, by ascribing to the way the attribute of its traveller, metaphorically. What is meant by this is clear.

On the authority of al-Suddi, the way here is the way out of the womb. This is not right at all.

Abu al-Sammal and Abu al-Aaj read *immā* with a *fatḥa* on the hamza in both places. This is a dialect (*lugha*) that Abu Zayd transmitted from the Arabs, and it is the particle that some people, as Abu Hayyan said, counted among the particles of conjunction (*ḥurūf al-ʿaṭf*). They cited the verse:

*They fertilise them, either a cold northern wind, or the eastern breeze blowing at the onset of dusk.*

Al-Zamakhshari took *immā* as the detailing particle that carries the sense of a condition, with the meaning: ﴿either grateful﴾, then by Our granting success (*tawfīq*); ﴿or ungrateful﴾, then by the evil of his own choice. He said this interpretation is an exposition of his school of thought. It was said: there is no objection to his taking it as an instance of ﴿He leads many astray thereby and guides many thereby﴾ (al-Baqarah: 26), as if it were said: ﴿either grateful﴾, then by Our guidance, that is, Our invitation or Our decrees, according to how guidance was explained. ﴿Or ungrateful﴾, then likewise by it, because the way of the invitation differs, since guidance here is not set against misguidance. This applies to both schools of thought and is free of omitting what has no evidence.

In al-Intisaf it was permitted that the meaning be: ﴿either grateful﴾, then he is rewarded; ﴿or ungrateful﴾, then he is punished. The use of the intensive form *kafūr* for the ungrateful is to observe the rhyme (*fawāṣil*), and to indicate that a person rarely escapes some form of ingratitude, and that what is held against him is only excessive disbelief.

Surah 76, verse 4: the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani)

﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾ (hayya'na, made ready) ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ from among the individuals of mankind who were guided to the path, ﴿chains﴾ by which they are led, ﴿and shackles﴾ by which they are bound, ﴿and a blazing fire﴾ by which they are burned. The mention of their threat before their (later) mention is for the purpose of combining the two in the recitation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turned black...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106], and so on. Also, warning is more fitting to the context and deserves attention. Also, it is better to begin and end the speech with mention of the believers, although describing them in detail might, if placed first, disrupt the harmony of the noble text's extremities.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and al-A'mash read ﴿سَلاسِلًا﴾ with tanwin (nunation) when continuing (wasl) and with the alif substituted for it when pausing (waqf). Al-Zamakhshari said: "In this there are two possibilities. The first is that this nun is a substitute for the vowel-lengthening letter (harf al-itlaq), and continuation takes the same form as pausing. The second is that the reciter is one who was accustomed to narrating poetry and whose tongue became used to giving diptote words the inflection of triptotes."

As for the first: substitution for vowel-lengthening letters outside poetry is rare, and it is further compounded by treating continuation like pause. As for the second: it permits reciting by personal preference without a sound basis in Arabic grammar. The point is that it was done for the sake of rhyme and matching (al-izdiwaj wa al-mushakalah), for they permitted for this purpose the inflection of what is not inflected, especially the plural, since it is a weak cause (for being diptote) because of its resemblance to the singular in its plural form, as in ﴿صَواحِباتِ يُوسُفَ﴾ and ﴿نَواكِسِي الأبْصارِ﴾. For this reason some of them permitted its inflection in all cases, as it has been said:

"Inflection in the plural has come often, until a people claimed it was optional."

Al-Akhfash related from a group of the Arabs that their dialect was to inflect every diptote except af'al (the comparative form). The inflected reading ﴿سَلاسِلًا﴾ is attested in the codices (masahif) of Madinah, Makkah, Kufa and Basra, and in the codices of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. Hisham related from Ibn 'Amir: ﴿سَلاسِلَ﴾ in continuation, and ﴿سَلاسِلًا﴾ with an alif, without tanwin, in pause.

**﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾** This begins an account of the good state of the grateful, following the account of the evil state of the disbelievers. They are introduced under the title of *al-birr* (righteousness) to indicate that the reason they attained the honour they received is what they deserved, and to renew the attribute of praise for them. *Al-abrar* is the plural of *barr*, like *rabb* and *arbab*, or of *barr* (the form *bar*), like *shahid* and *ashhad*, based on the view that the plural pattern *af'al* is used for *fa'il*. *Al-barr* means one who is obedient and who abounds in doing good. It was also said that it means one who fulfils the right of God the Exalted and fulfils his vows. It is reported from al-Hasan that it means the one who does not harm an ant and does not desire evil.

**﴿will drink﴾** in the Hereafter **﴿from a cup﴾** *Ka's* (cup), as al-Zajjaj said, is the vessel when it contains drink; when it does not, it is not called a *ka's*. Al-Raghib said: *al-ka's* is the vessel together with what is in it of drink, and each of the two is called a *ka's* when it stands alone. The well-known view is that the word is used literally for the glass when there is wine in it, and figuratively for the wine itself, by the relation of contiguity (*'alaqa al-mujawara*, a figurative link based on proximity). The intended meaning here is said to be the wine, in which case *min* (from) is partitive or explanatory. It was also said that it means the glass in which the wine is, in which case *min* is for the starting point. The statement of God the Exalted **﴿whose mixture is camphor﴾** fits the first view better. Apparently this is in the pattern of **﴿God was ever Knowing, Wise﴾** [An-Nisa: 17 and elsewhere], and the use of the verb is for affirmation and permanence. It was also said that *kana* (was) is complete (meaning "came to be") from the statement of God the Exalted **﴿"Be," and it is﴾** [Al-Baqarah: 117 and elsewhere]. *Al-mizaj* is that with which something is mixed, like *al-hizam* (belt) for that with which something is girded; so it is a noun of instrument. *Kafur*, as al-Kalbi said, is the name of a spring in Paradise whose water is like camphor in whiteness, scent and coolness. It is left uninflected (*suriffa*) to match the rhyme of the verses. The sentence is understood with an omitted modifier, meaning "water of camphor." The clause is an attribute of **﴿cup﴾**. This view goes against the apparent meaning, and perhaps if no report is authentic regarding it, it is not accepted.

Abdullah read **«qafuran»** with a *qaf* in place of the *kaf*, and these two letters often alternate within a word, as in the saying of the Arabs *'arabiyyun quhhun* and *kahhun* (pure Arab).

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 76, verse 6:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿a spring﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for *kafur* (camphor). Qatadah said: "He mixes it for them with camphor and seals it for them with musk, because of camphor's coolness, whiteness, and pleasant fragrance." So *kafur* keeps its familiar meaning. It has also been said that God, when He created the wine of Paradise, deposited in it the praiseworthy qualities of camphor, so its being a mixture is a figurative usage (*majaz*) in attributing those qualities to it. On these two views, ﴿a spring﴾ is in apposition to the position (*mahall*) of *ka's* (cup), with an omitted noun (*mudaf*) implied, meaning: they drink wine, the wine of a spring. Or it is in the accusative of specification (*ikhtisas*) by an implied verb, "I mean" or "I specify," as al-Mubarrad said. It has also been said that it is in the circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿its mixture﴾. It has also been said that it is from *ka's* (cup), and the description of it was permitted, meaning that it is described as abundant and clear. It has also been said that it is governed by a verb implied by what follows, namely His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from which the servants of God drink﴾, again with an omitted noun, meaning: they drink the water of a spring from which they drink, and so on.

It was objected that the clause is a description (*sifah*) of ﴿a spring﴾, so its verb does not govern it, and what does not govern cannot explain a governing verb. The reply is that on this reading it is not a description, and the construction is like *rajulan darabtuhu* (a man, I struck him). Yes, it is a description of a spring on another reading. The *ba'* (with) here indicates association (*ilsaq*), not transitivity (*ta'diyah*), and it is semantically connected to an omitted element, meaning: they drink the wine mixed with it, that is with the spring, ﴿the servants of God﴾. This is like your saying, "I drank the water with honey." This applies when camphor is taken as the proper name of a spring in Paradise. As for the other two views, it has been said that the function of the *ba'* is to make the statement belong to the construction of the line:

*yajrahu fi 'araqibiha nasli*
(he wounds in their hamstrings my sword)

for the sake of emphasis (*mubalaghah*). It has also been said that the *ba'* marks transitivity, and *yashrabu* (drinks) is taken to mean *yarwa* (quenches), so it takes *bi-*. It has also been said that it means *min* (from). It has been said that it is redundant (*za'idah*), and the meaning is "they drink it," as in the words of al-Hazli:

*sharibna bi-ma'i al-bahri thumma taraffa'at*
*mata luhaju khudrin lahunna na'iju*
(They drank the water of the sea, then rose up, whenever the green deep waves had a roar for them.)

This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abi Abla, *"yashrabuha"* (they drink it). It has also been said that the pronoun in *bi-ha* refers to the cup, and the meaning is: they drink the spring with that cup. On this view, ﴿a spring﴾ may be the object of *yashrabu*, with the phrase placed before it, and ﴿the servants of God﴾ means the believers, the people of Paradise.

﴿They make it gush forth in abundance﴾ is another description of ﴿a spring﴾, meaning: they channel it wherever they wish from their dwellings, with easy channeling that nothing prevents them from. The indefiniteness (*tankir*) is for variety (*tanwi'*).

Abdullah ibn Ahmad recorded in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, from Ibn Shawzab, that he said: "They have rods of gold with which they channel it, and the water follows their rods." In some reports: "This spring, in the house of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), flows to the houses of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the believers."

﴿They fulfil their vows﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), brought in to explain the reason they are granted this bliss. It contains a kind of detailed elaboration of what the term "the righteous" (al-abrar) indicates in general, as if it were said: "What do they do so that they attain that lofty rank?" It was answered: "They fulfil..." etc. I would add that it is a resumptive sentence for explanation. Along with this, the discourse shifted from the perfect (awfa) to the imperfect (al-mudari') for vividness (al-istihdar) and to indicate continuity. Fulfilling the vow is a metonymy (kinayah) for performing all the obligations, and the knowledge of what lies beyond them follows a fortiori (al-tariq al-awla), and by the indication of the text (ishārat al-nass), for whoever fulfils what he has obligated upon himself, fulfilling what God Most High has obligated upon him is more important to him and more fitting. Taking this as a metonymy is what is required by what has been related from Qatadah, Ikrimah and Mujahid, while leaving it on its apparent meaning is what they said: that is, if they vow an act of obedience, they perform it. ﴿And they fear a Day whose evil [i.e., its punishment] was ﴾ widespread, ﴿spreading far and wide﴾ in every direction, to the utmost extent of dispersal, from istatara al-harīq (the fire spread) and al-fajr (the dawn spread), and it is more intensive than tara (to fly), because the increase in the form (al-mabna) indicates an increase in meaning. The imperative mood also has an indication of this, because what is sought should be emphasized. In their being described with this there is an indication of the goodness of their creed and their avoidance of sins.

﴿And they give food, despite their love for it﴾: that is, while they are loving the food, meaning together with their desire for it and their need of it. This is of the type of *tatmim* (completion, a rhetorical device in which a phrase is completed to add emphasis). The Qur'an corroborates this meaning in the words of God Most High: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, or [the meaning is] "despite their love of giving food," that it is done with good will and without affectation. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl adopted this view, and it is a good one. Or [the meaning is] "while they are loving God Most High," or "giving food that is [done] out of love for Him, for His sake, seeking His pleasure, may He be glorified and exalted." Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad and Abu Sulayman al-Darani adopted this view.

"'Ala hubbihi" [in this sense] is of the type of *takmil* (completion). Some scholars declared it unsound and said that the first [interpretation] is the correct one. The Qur'an corroborates it, since in the words of God Most High "for the sake of God" that follows there is a sufficiency from His saying "for the sake of God" [again]. There is room for consideration in this; rather, it is perhaps the more appropriate for that. The mention of "food" although giving food suffices for it is to specify the referent of the pronoun according to the first [interpretation], and because food is like knowledge in that it is what sustains the body, the soundness of the constitution, and the preservation of the self. So stating it explicitly emphasizes the magnificence of their act according to the latter two [interpretations]. It may also be considered so according to the first.

Then, the apparent meaning is that "giving food" is meant in its literal sense.

It has also been said that it is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for kindness toward the needy and comforting them in whatever way, even if it is not with food itself. It is as if they benefit [others] in every kind of benefit. ﴿A needy person, an orphan, and a captive﴾. It has been said: any captive whatsoever. Al-Hasan related that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to be brought a captive, and he would hand him over to one of the Muslims, saying: "Be good to him." So he would keep him for two or three days, and he would give him preference over himself.

Qatadah said: their captives on that day were polytheists, and "your Muslim brother is more deserving that you feed him." Ibn 'Asakir related from Mujahid that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned with the captives from Badr, seven of the Emigrants, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Ali, al-Zubayr, 'Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd, and Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, spent on the captives of the polytheists of Badr. The Helpers said: 'We killed them for God and for His Messenger (ﷺ), and you help them with provision?' So God revealed concerning them nineteen verses: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink﴾ up to His saying ﴿a spring within it called Salsabil﴾ [Al-Insan: 5–18]." In this there is evidence that feeding captives, even if they are from among the people of polytheism, is good and its reward is hoped for. As for the first report, Ibn Hajar said: no one whom the people of hadith rely upon has mentioned it. Ibn al-'Iraqi said: I have not found it. As for the second report, I have not seen it transmitted by any single narrator other than Ibn 'Asakir, and I have no confidence in its authenticity. It implies that these verses are Medinan, and you already know the disagreement on that. Yes, according to the majority of scholars, it is permissible to do good to disbelievers within the abode of Islam, and obligatory charities are not given to them.

Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' said: it is the captive from among the People of the Qiblah. Al-Tibi said: this is only correct if the feeding happened in the abode of war, by a Muslim toward a captive in their hands. It has been said: it is the Muslim captive who was left in the lands of the disbelievers as a hostage and went out seeking ransom.

Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) transmitted from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and 'Ata' that they said: it is the imprisoned person from among the People of the Qiblah. In this there is evidence that feeding the families of imprisoned Muslims is good. It may be said: feeding the imprisoned is not good if he is withholding a debt he is able to repay, for he only refrains from it out of obstinacy and for some worldly aim of the self.

It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it is the slave and the imprisoned. Calling the imprisoned one a captive is a metaphor (*majaz*), because he is prevented from going out. As for calling the slave [a captive], it is also a metaphor, but it has been said that it is by consideration of what he was, and it has been said that it is by consideration of his resemblance to the captive in being restricted by the bonds of command and in not being able to do what he desires. Counting the creditor as a captive is based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Your creditor is your captive, so be good to your captive." This is an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), except that what was said about the first report has been said about this report as well. Abu Hamzah al-Yamani said: it is the wife, and its weakness here is evident.

صفحة 156

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, we feed you only for the sake of Allah's Countenance﴾. This is according to the supposition of a statement that occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of ﴿yut'imūna﴾ (they feed) — meaning, saying that by the tongue of circumstance (lisān al-ḥāl), because of the signs of sincerity that appear upon them. And on the authority of Mujahid: "Either they did not actually speak it, but Allah, exalted is He, knew it from them, so He praised them for it, so that one who desires it might be eager for it"; or [it was said] by the tongue of speech (lisān al-maqāl), to remove the suspicion of reproach (mann), which nullifies charity, and the expectation of recompense, which diminishes the reward. And on the authority of al-Ṣiddīqa (may Allah be pleased with her): that she used to send charity to a household, then she would ask the Messenger (ﷺ) what they had said; and whenever he mentioned a supplication, she would supplicate for them with its like, so that the reward of the charity would remain pure for her with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It is also permissible that their saying this was for them a gentle instruction, a teaching of understanding, and an admonition regarding what one who is sincere to Allah, exalted is He, ought to be upon; but it is not that. And His statement, exalted is He, ﴿We do not desire from you any recompense﴾ by deeds ﴿nor thanks﴾, nor gratitude and praise by words, is a confirmation and emphasis of what came before it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day⟩ i.e., the punishment of a Day; so it is by way of an elided noun (muḍāf), or his fear is a metonymy for fear of what is in it. ﴿Austere⟩ (ʿabūsan), a Day in which faces frown. This is taken as a figurative attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī), as in "his day is fasting" (nahāruhu ṣāʾimun). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the disbeliever will frown on that day until sweat flows from between his eyes like tar, or he resembles a frowning lion. This is taken as a personification metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-makniyya al-takhyīliyya). But it is not hidden that frowning is not one of the attributes of the lion; rather, it is well known as a description of it, so there is some weakness in the takhyīliyya. It was also said that it is a eloquent simile (al-tashbīh al-balīgh). ﴿Intensely austere⟩ (qamṭarīran): very severely frowning. It is said: hard and difficult, as if its evil has wrapped its parts around one another. It was also said: long, and this is a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has also come as qamāṭir, and they recited for Asad ibn Nāghiṣa:

I have endured wars every day, brave in evil, harsh in morning,
O sons of our paternal uncles, do you remember our trials for you when there was a qamāṭir day?

And another opinion:

Al-Zajjaj went to the first view and said: al-qamṭarīr is one who frowns until the space between his eyes gathers. It is said: iqmaṭarrat the she-camel when she raises her tail, clamps her nose, and gathers her two sides (quṭrayhā), i.e., her two flanks, as if she does this when she reaches old age, or when she is about to deliver her offspring. According to him its derivation, by the greater derivation (al-ishtiqāq al-kabīr), is from quṭr, with the mīm being augmentative. This does not bind al-Zajjaj, so it is permissible that it be derived in this way from qamaṭ, and it is said: qamaṭahu when he tied it and gathered its ends. In al-Baḥr it is said: iqmaṭarra, so he is muqmaṭirr and qamṭarīr and qumāṭir when it became difficult and severe. The form of this pattern is disputed, and most grammarians do not affirm ifmaʿalla as a verbal pattern. This clause has been permitted to be a cause for their beneficence and their stated action, as if it were said: we do for you what we do because we fear a Day whose description is such and such, so we hope by that that our Lord, majestic and exalted, will protect us from its evil. It may also be a cause for not desiring recompense or thanks, i.e., we do not want from you reward in seeking compensation through charity, because of fear of the punishment of God, exalted. Al-Kashshaf alludes to both aspects, and in al-Kashf it says: the second is more apt, so that His saying "for the sake of God" remains pure, not mixed with a share of the self from attracting benefit or repelling harm. If it were made a cause of the feeding that is itself explained by the meaning "we specified the beneficence for His sake only because we fear the Day of His recompense, and whoever fears Him adheres to sincerity," it would also be a valid view.

"So Allah protected them from the evil of that Day" (﴿فَوَقاهُمُ اللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَلِكَ اليَوْمِ﴾), on account of their fear and their guarding themselves against it.

Abu Ja'far read فَوَقّاهم with a doubled qaf (fa-waqqāhum), and this is more fitting with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He gave them radiance and joy﴾ (﴿ولَقّاهم نَضْرَةً وسُرُورًا﴾), meaning: He gave them, in place of the frowning and grief of the wicked, radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 12:

﴿And He will reward them for what they endured with a garden and silk﴾: for their patience in the hardships of acts of obedience and in restraining their desires by avoiding what is forbidden and preferring others over their own wealth in food and clothing. ﴿A garden﴾: a great orchard from which they eat whatever they wish. ﴿And silk﴾: which they wear and with which they adorn themselves.

From the narration of 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, that al-Hasan and al-Husayn fell ill, and their grandfather Muhammad (ﷺ) visited them, along with Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them), and the Companions who visited them also came. They said to 'Ali (may Allah honor his face): "O Abu al-Hasan, if only you would make a vow on behalf of your two sons." So 'Ali, Fatimah, and their servant Fidda made a vow that if they recovered from what they had, they would fast three days in thanks. Then Allah clothed the two boys in the garment of health.

The household of Muhammad had nothing, little or much. So 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) went to Shim'un the Jew of Khaybar and borrowed three sa' of barley from him. He brought it back, and Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) stood up to a sa', ground it, and baked from it five loaves, one for each of them. 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) prayed the maghrib prayer with the Prophet (ﷺ), then came to the house and placed the food before them. A beggar stood at the door and said: "Peace be upon you, O people of the House of Muhammad (ﷺ). I am a poor man from the poor of the Muslims. Feed me, and Allah will feed you from the banquets of Paradise." So they gave him preference, and they spent the night having tasted nothing but water, and they awoke fasting. Then Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) stood up to another sa', ground it, and baked it. 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) prayed the maghrib prayer with the Prophet (ﷺ), then came to the house and placed the food before them. An orphan stood at the door and said: "Peace be upon you, O people of the House of Muhammad (ﷺ). I am an orphan from the children of the emigrants. Feed me, and Allah will feed you from the banquets of Paradise." So they gave him preference, and they remained two days and two nights having tasted nothing but plain water, and they awoke fasting. When the third day came, Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) stood up to the third sa', ground it, and baked it. 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) prayed the maghrib prayer with the Prophet (ﷺ), then came to the house and placed the food before them. A captive stood at the door and said: "Peace be upon you, O people of the House of Muhammad (ﷺ). I am a captive of Muhammad, may blessings and peace be upon him. Feed me, and Allah will feed you." So they gave him preference, and they spent the night having tasted nothing but plain water.

When they awoke, 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) took al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He saw them trembling like young birds from the intensity of hunger, and he said: "O Abu al-Hasan, how grievous it is to me to see you in this state!" He stood and went with them to Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her). He found her in her prayer niche, her belly clinging to her back and her eyes sunken from the intensity of hunger. He (ﷺ) was moved by this and was distressed by it. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and said: "Take it, O Muhammad. May Allah give you joy in your household." He said: "And what shall I take, O Gabriel?" He said: "Recite to him: ﴿Has there come upon man...﴾" – the surah.

In the narration of Ibn Mahran: "The Prophet (ﷺ) leapt up until he entered upon Fatimah, and he bent over her weeping. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended with this verse: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink...﴾" to its end. In a narration from 'Ata': "The barley was the wage for irrigating palm trees, and a third of it was made into porridge each day, and they gave their portion to others."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and they feed...﴾ etc.: "It was revealed concerning 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) and Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and upon them [may Allah bless them and grant them peace]." He did not mention the story, though the report is well known among people. Al-Wahidi mentioned it in his book al-Basit, and upon it is the saying of some of the Shi'ah:

How long shall I be blamed, and until when shall I be reproached for loving this young man?
Has Fatimah been married to anyone other than him? And in someone other than him, has there come, has there come?

It has been objected that it is a fabricated (mawdu') and invented report, as al-Tirmidhi and Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned, and the marks of fabrication are evident in it, both in wording and in meaning. Furthermore, it implies that the surah is Medinan, because 'Ali's (may Allah honor his face) marriage to Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) took place in Medina. Yet according to Ibn 'Abbas, from whom it is narrated, as al-Nahhas reported, it is Meccan, and likewise according to the majority in one opinion.

I say: the question of whether it is Meccan or Medinan is greatly disputed, as you have heard, so there is no certainty about it. Ibn al-Jawzi transmitted the report in his Tabsirah without objecting to it, yet he is among those who are lenient regarding fabrication, to the point that they said he should not be relied upon in this field. Thus, the possibility that the original revelation concerned the Commander (may Allah honor his face) and Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) remains open, and there is no firm affirmation or denial, because the reports conflict, and the preferred view is hardly free from dispute. Yes, perhaps it is more likely that the manner described in the first narration did not occur. Furthermore, even on the view that it was revealed concerning the two of them, its ruling is not restricted to them but includes everyone who does the like, as al-Tabarsi, a Shi'ite, mentioned in Majma' al-Bayan, transmitting it from 'Abd Allah ibn Maymun, from Abu 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him). And on the view that it was not revealed concerning them, their station is not diminished and their rank is not lessened, for their inclusion among the righteous is clear, indeed it is a more fitting inclusion. So they are what they are, and what can a man say about them except that 'Ali is the master of the believers and the successor of the Prophet, and Fatimah is the Ahmadi part and the Muhammadan portion. As for the two sons, they are the spirit and the fragrance, and the lords of the youths of Paradise. This is not from rafd (Shi'i extremism) in any way; rather, whatever else is, in my view, error:

I am a servant of the Truth, not a servant of desire;
May Allah curse desire in whomever He curses.

Among the subtleties, on the view that it was revealed concerning them, is that He, glorified is He, did not mention the Huris (al-hur al-'in) in it, but rather explicitly mentioned "youths who remain forever," out of regard for the sanctity of the virgin (al-batul) and the coolness of the Messenger's eye, lest her natural jealousy be stirred if she sensed a co-wife, even in the imagination of human nature, even if only once in Paradise. It is not hidden from you that this is a flower of spring which does not bear rubbing. Then, the masculine form of reference here is also by way of taghlib (the grammatical convention of giving precedence to the masculine).

'Ali (may Allah honor his face) recited it as "jaza'hum" (جازاهُمْ), on the pattern of fa'ala.

﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to "they" in "their reward," and the governing verb is "jazā" (He rewarded). This particular state is singled out for the reward because it is the most complete state of one enjoying comfort. The Almighty's words ﴿because they endured﴾ do not conflict with this, since the endurance is in this world, and what is consequent upon it is in the Hereafter. It is also said that it is a description of the Garden. The pronoun was not made explicit, even though the description applies to other than the one it describes, so one does not say "reclining they therein," to avoid ambiguity, as in the verse:

"My people are the pinnacles of glory, whose builders are known; ʿAdnān and Qaḥṭān know the reality of that."

You know this. The view of the Kufan school of grammar (al-Kūfiyyah) and the doctrine of the Basran school (al-Baṣriyyah) is that the pronoun must be made explicit in such cases without exception, and the verse in question involves a discussion. It is also said that it may be a future circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah) from the pronoun in ﴿they endured﴾, but this is not correct.

"Al-arā'ik" is the plural of "arīkah," which is a couch in a canopied enclosure (ḥajlah) that has a curtain around it. It is not called an "arīkah" when it stands alone. It is also said that it is anything one reclines upon, whether a couch, a bed, or a raised seat. Its being named thus is because it is a place of residence, taken from their saying "araka bi-l-makān, ʾurūkan," meaning he stayed in the place. The root meaning of "al-ʾurūk" is staying in order to graze on the "arāk," which is the well-known tree, and then the word was used for other kinds of staying.

The Almighty's words ﴿they see therein no sun nor bitter cold﴾ are either a second circumstantial clause from the pronoun, or a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in ﴿reclining﴾. It is also permitted that it be a description of "Garden." The meaning is that its air is temperate, with no scorching heat of the sun that burns nor severe cold that harms. In a ḥadīth: "The air of Paradise is sajsaj (temperate), neither hot nor cold." Thus by negating the sun, it intends to negate both it and its consequence together, given His words, glorified be He, ﴿nor bitter cold﴾. It is as if it were said: they see therein neither heat nor cold.

It is also said that "al-zamharīr" is the moon. It is related from Tha'lab that it is in the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ, and he recited:

"A night whose darkness has gathered thickly, its pieces and al-zamharīr, which has shone."

This does not mean that its nature is cold, as some have said, because it is in the realm of prevention. Rather it has been said that it proved that all lights are hot. It is possible that this is because of its brightness, taking it from "izdamharra al-kawkab," meaning the star shone. The meaning according to this view is that its air is luminous in itself, not needing a sun or a moon.

In a ḥadīth: "Indeed Paradise has no equal, by the Lord of the Ka'bah, it is light that gleams, a fragrant plant that sways, and a lofty palace." The ḥadīth. Then, despite this, a light stronger than its own light may appear in it, as the authentic reports attest. In some reports from Ibn ʿAbbās: While the people of Paradise were in Paradise, they saw a light like the light of the sun, and the gardens were illuminated by it. The people of Paradise said: "O Riḍwān, what is this, when our Lord has said ﴿they see therein no sun nor bitter cold﴾?" Riḍwān says to them: "This is not a sun nor a moon, but ʿAlī and Fāṭimah, may Allah be pleased with them both, laughed, and the gardens were illuminated by the light of their two teeth."

﴿And its shades drooping over them, near﴾ is coordinated with the preceding clause, and its circumstantial state (ḥāl) is the same state, or it is a qualifier (ṣifah) of an omitted noun coordinated with "a garden" earlier, meaning: and another garden, with its shades near over them, on the basis that they were promised two gardens, as in His saying, ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 46]. Abū Ḥaywa read "dāniyatun" (دانِيَةٌ) with a nominative ending, and it was explained that "dāniyatun" is a predicate (khabar) placed before its subject, "ẓilāluhā" (ظِلالُها), and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state, on the basis that the wāw is conjunctive or circumstantial, or in the position of a qualifier, on the basis that the wāw is also conjunctive, or that it is for attachment (lil-ilṣāq), according to what al-Zamakhsharī holds.

Al-Akhfash said that "ẓilāluhā" is nominative as the agent (fā'il) of "dāniyatin," and he used this as evidence for the permissibility of the active participle (ism al-fā'il) acting without a preceding word (i'timād), as in "qā'imun al-zaydūna" (قائِمٌ الزَّيْدُونَ). You know that this is not fit for use as evidence, because of the possibility that it is a predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), so that it depends on something: that is, "wa-hiya dāniyatun 'alayhim ẓilāluhā" (وهي دانِيَةٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ظِلالُها), meaning "and it is near over them, its shades." Ubayy read "wa-dānin" (ودِانٍ) like "qāḍin," and the evidence does not complete for al-Akhfash by it either, though there is some difference between it and what came before.

Al-A'mash read "wa-dāniyan 'alayhim" (ودانِيًا عَلَيْهِمْ), like "khāshi'an abṣāruhum" (خاشِعًا أبْصارُهم). The meaning is that the shades of the trees of the Garden are near to the righteous, a canopy over them, as an increase in their bliss.

﴿And its clusters are made easy to reach, making them easy﴾. That is, its fruits are subjected to the one who reaches for them, and its taking is easy, from "dhull" (the root meaning ease), which is the opposite of difficulty. Qatāda, Mujāhid and Sufyān said: if the person is standing, he takes the fruit without hardship, and if he is sitting or lying down, it is likewise. So this is its making easy: no distance and no thorn turns the hand away from it. The clause is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (dāniyatan) (دانِيَةً), meaning: its shades draw near over them, making its clusters easy for them, or it is coordinated with what precedes it, and it is a verbal clause coordinated with a nominal one in the reading "dāniyatun" with a nominative ending. The point of the difference is that the continuance of the shade is desired there, while the renewal of the making easy of the clusters is according to need.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 15:

﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels⟩ (āniyah), the plural of ināʾ (a container), like kisāʾ (cloak) and aksiyah (cloaks); it is that in which a thing is placed. And awāniy is the plural of the plural. ﴿Of silver and goblets⟩ (akwāb), the plural of kūb, which is a cup without a handle, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said. In the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit, the lexicon of al-Fayruzabadi) it says: a jug without a handle, or without a spout. It has also been said: the kūz is a large jug that has neither a handle nor an ear. ﴿They were⟩ (kānat), i.e., those goblets ﴿crystal-clear⟩ (qawārīr), the plural of qārūrah, which is a thin container made of glass in which drinks are placed. Its being in the accusative (naṣbuhu) is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) if kānat is complete (tāmmah), and it is as when you say: "qawārīr were created."

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 16:

Allah's saying ﴿crystal-like vessels of silver﴾ is a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution) and the expression is an eloquent simile (al-tashbih al-baligh). The meaning is that they were formed combining the clearness and translucency of glass with the smoothness and whiteness of silver. Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until it became like the wing of a fly, the water would not be seen behind it. But the crystal vessels of Paradise are of the whiteness of silver together with the clearness of crystal." Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: "There is nothing in Paradise except that you have been given its likeness in this world, except the crystal vessels of silver."

Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read «qawarira» with tanwin (nunation) in both places when pausing and in continuous recitation, and change it to an alif when stopping. Ibn Kathir prevents the second from taking tanwin (it is diptote, mamnu' min al-sarf) and lets the first take it, because it occurs at the fasila (verse-end rhyme) and at the end of the verse. He stopped on it with an alif to harmonize it (mushakala) with the other words of the verse-endings. According to al-Zamakhshari, the tanwin on the first is a substitute for the alif of extension (alif al-itlaq), as in the verse:

Oh friend, what stirred the eyes to weep so much?

And the tanwin on the second is for conformity (li'l-ittiba'), so reflect on this. The reading with prevention of declension for both (mana' al-sarf) belongs to Hafs, Ibn Amir, Hamza and Abu Amr. Al-A'mash read the second «qawarir» in the nominative, meaning: they are crystal vessels.

﴿They have determined them with determination﴾ means: they determined those crystal vessels within themselves, so they came exactly as they had determined, with no addition beyond that, and it is not possible for anything to be added to it. The meaning of this is the saying of al-Ta'i:

Even if you were to portray yourself, you would not add to it
Anything beyond the noble qualities of character that are in you.

This indicates that his self was created in the most perfect form of praiseworthy attributes, such that nothing can be added to it.

[Page 160]

The pronoun in ﴿qaddarūhā﴾ refers to the righteous who are being served (al-abrar al-mutāf 'alayhim), or it means: they determined its drink according to the measure of satisfaction, which is the most delightful to the drinker. Ibn Abbas said: "They brought it in accordance with the need; they do not prefer anything and do not desire anything after it." And from Mujahid, its determination is that it is neither full to overflowing nor deficient so that it empties. So the pronoun, according to what is apparent, refers to the cupbearers who go around with it, which is implied by Allah's saying (they are served with it).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The cupbearers determined it." It was also said: the meaning is that they determined it by their righteous deeds, so it came according to their measure. The pronoun in this case is said to refer to the angels, and it is also said to refer to the cupbearers.

Ali, may Allah honor his face, Ibn Abbas, al-Sulami, al-Sha'bi, Qatada, Zayd ibn Ali, al-Jahdari, al-Asma'i from Abu Amr, Ibn Abd al-Khaliq from Ya'qub, and others read «quddirūhā» in the passive voice. Its grammatical analysis (takhrij) has been disputed. Abu Ali said: the original wording was "qaddarū 'alayhā" (they determined over it). In al-Mughni there is inversion (qalb), because the real form should be "qadirtu 'alayhim" (I was able over them). It is like Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, its keys would burden a band of strong men﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and the Arabs' saying: when al-Jawza' (Orion) rises, the stick rises over the chameleon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the way of understanding this is that it comes from qadartu al-shay' (with the light form), meaning "I specified its measure," which was then transferred to the intensive form (al-taf'il), and so it became transitive to two objects: one is the pronoun that substitutes for the subject (na'ib al-fa'il), and the second is "ha." The meaning is that they were made able over them as they wished, and they were permitted to determine according to what they desired. Abu Hatim said: "The vessels were determined according to the measure of their satisfaction." Some explained this by saying that there is an ellipsis in the sentence, namely that there was "qadr" (a measure) according to the measure of their satisfaction from them, so "ʿalā" was deleted and "qadr" became the substitute for the subject; then it was deleted, and their "rayy" (satisfaction) became the substitute for the subject; then it was deleted and they became the substitute for the subject, and the second object was joined to "qadr," so it became "qadruhā." Abu Hayyan said: the closer view is that the original was "qadr rayyihim minhā taqdīran," so the genitive (al-mudāf) which is "al-rayy" was deleted and the pronoun was put in its place, so it became "qaddarū minhā"; then the verb was extended, "min" was deleted, and the verb reached the pronoun directly, so it became "qaddarūhā." There was thus no more than the deletion of a mudaf and an extension in the genitive complement.

It is not hidden that the inversion is a flawed view, and what some have established is extremely forced. As for whether what Abu Hayyan chose is closer than what Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) chose, there is room for consideration, and perhaps it is even more forced than that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verses 17–18:**

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾ ﴿a spring therein named Salsabil﴾. Most of what was said regarding His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿They will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾ applies here, "etc.", in terms of the aspects (of meaning) and the ginger. Al-Dinawari said: "It is a plant in the land of Oman. It is roots that spread through the land, and it is not a tree. Some of it is imported from the lands of the Zanj and China, and this is the finest. The Arabs loved it because when it is mixed into drink it causes a stinging on the tongue, so they find pleasure in it. For this reason they mention it in describing the saliva of women." Al-A'sha said:

*As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and aryy (a sweet honey-drink) poured out in a cup.*

Amr ibn al-Musayyab ibn 'Alas said:

*As if the taste of ginger were in it, when you tasted it, and the pure essence of wine.*

Some of the grammarians counted it among the *mu'rabat* (words inflected by i'rab, grammatical case endings). That ginger is the name of a spring in Paradise is narrated from Qatadah, who said: "The ones brought near will drink from it pure, and it will be mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise." The apparent meaning is that they will sometimes drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor, and sometimes be given to drink from a cup whose mixture is ginger. Perhaps the mention of ﴿they will be given to drink﴾ here, rather than ﴿they will drink﴾, is because it is more fitting to what precedes it, His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And there will be circulated among them﴾, etc. It is also possible that there is an allusion in it that this cup is higher in rank than the first cup.

It is narrated from al-Kalbi: "It is given to drink from two cups. The first is mixed with camphor, and the second is mixed with ginger." *Salsabil* is like *salsal* and *salsal* (both meaning smooth, flowing). Al-Zajjaj said: "It is the drink that is most extreme in smoothness and ease of passage down the throat." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "I have not heard *salsabil* except in the Qur'an." It seems that the spring was named thus for its smoothness and the ease with which it is swallowed. 'Ikrimah said: "A spring whose water is *salsal* (smooth, flowing)." Mujahid said: "A quickly flowing, smooth channel, easy to swallow." Muqatil said: "A spring whose water flows smoothly over them in their gatherings however they wish." According to what is narrated from Qatadah, it is a spring that gushes from beneath the Throne, from the Garden of Eden, flowing smoothly into the gardens.

[Page 161]

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), it says: "The apparent meaning is that this spring is named *Salsabil* in the sense that it is described as smooth to swallow and easy in taste. *Salsabil* should not be taken as a proper name, for in that case it would be non-declinable (*mamnu' al-sarf*) due to feminine gender and proper-noun status. It is narrated from Talhah that he read it without the *alif*, making it a proper noun for it. If it is a proper noun, then the reading of the majority, with *tanwin* (nunation), is appropriate to the rhyme endings, as was said regarding *salasila* and *qawarira*." Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the letter *ba'* was added to it so that the word became quinquiliteral (five-lettered). If he means that it was actually added, then this is not sound, because *ba'* is not among the familiar letters of augmentation. If he means that it is a letter that came within the structure of the word, and it is not present in *salsal* or *silsal*, then this is correct, and it would be one of those words whose meaning agrees while their root differs, and it ends (the quotation of al-Bahr).

In al-Kashshaf, it says: "He does not mean the technical augmentation. Do you not see his saying 'until it became quinquiliteral'? And this is also from *al-ishtiqaq al-akbar* (the major derivation, in which roots share meaning through permutation of letters), so do not be heedless."

Some of the grammarians said: "*Salsabila* is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community to ask the way (*sabil*) to it." They attributed this to Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. This is not sound in its outward sense, unless it is intended that the whole phrase of the speaker, ﴿Salsabila﴾, was made the name of the spring, as it was said *Ta'abbata Sharran* and *Dhura Hubban*. It was named thus because no one drinks from it except one who has found his way to it through righteous deeds. Yet even if it is correct in Arabic, it is forced and innovative. Attributing it to someone like the Amir (Ali), may Allah ennoble his face, is more innovative still, and some stated explicitly that it is a fabrication against him, may Allah ennoble his face.

In the poetry of Ibn Mutran al-Shashi:

*Salsabilan therein, for the ease of the soul, with a wine as if it were Salsabil.*

In it is *al-jinas al-mulaffaq* (compound paronomasia, a play on words composed of two or more words), which many of the later poets also used.
