Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 19:

﴿And there will circulate among them youths of everlasting youth﴾, i.e., for service. ﴿Youths of everlasting youth﴾, i.e., they remain forever in the freshness and radiance they are in. It has also been said that they are adorned with earrings of khaladah, which is a kind of earring.

And there has come in a hadith narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, they are a thousand servants."

In some reports, it is multiples of that.

Generosity is greater and bounties are wider, and this varies in few and many according to the differing deeds of those served. ﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾, because of their beauty, the purity of their complexions, the brightness of their faces, their being dispersed throughout their gatherings and dwellings, and the reflection of the rays of some of them onto others. It has also been said that they are likened to moist pearls when scattered from their shell, because it is the finest and has the most lustre. According to this, it is a simile of the singular, since the dispersal is not what is intended. The address in ﴿you saw them﴾ is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who stands before it. Likewise in His, the Exalted's, saying.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 20:**

﴿And when you look there﴾, meaning: there, that is, in Paradise. It is in the accusative position as an adverb of place (*zarf*). The verb *ra'ayta* ("you see") is used as an intransitive verb (*munazzal manzilat al-lazim*), so it conveys generality in the context of address. The meaning is that wherever your sight falls in Paradise, ﴿you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾, of great magnitude, which no expression can encompass, and which includes both the sensible and the intelligible.

Abdullah ibn 'Amr al-Kalbi said: "Spacious and wide. The one of them with the lowest rank in Paradise will see in a dominion a distance of a thousand years. He will see its farthest part as he sees its nearest, because of the keenness of sight that he is given. Or it is one of the special features of Paradise."

Mujahid said: "It is the seeking of permission by the angels, peace be upon them, so they do not enter upon them except with permission."

al-Tirmidhi said: "I think, as Abu Hayyan al-Hakim thought, not Abu 'Isa the traditionist, author of the *al-Jami'*, that it is the dominion of creation and will: when they desire a thing, it occurs." It has also been said that it is the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it has been said other than that. It has also been said that it is the lasting dominion that has no end.

al-Farra' claimed that the meaning is: "And when you see what is there, you see..." etc. He interpreted it as meaning that *thamma* is an adverb of place for an omitted verb, which occurs as a relative clause (*sila*) of an omitted relative pronoun (*mawsul*), which is the object of *ra'ayta*. The estimate is: "And when you see what is there, you see bliss," etc. So *ma* was omitted, as it is omitted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly your bonds have been cut off among you﴾ [al-An'am: 94], meaning *ma baynakum* ("what is between you"). al-Zajjaj then, followed by al-Zamakhshari, criticized this as an error, because it is not permissible to drop the relative pronoun and leave its relative clause. You know that the Kufans permit this, and from it is the line of verse:

*"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and praises him, and supports him, is equal [in the same position]."*

He meant "and whoever praises him," so he omitted the relative pronoun and kept its relative clause. It may be said that this would be an objection only if he intended that the relative pronoun was assumed. But if he intended the meaning that the adverb of place takes the place of the direct object, then it is a sound statement, because the adverb of place and the thing seen are both Paradise.

Hamid al-A'raj read ﴿*thumma*﴾ with a *damma* on the *tha'*, as a conjunction of coordination (*harf 'atf*). The answer to *idha* ("when"), on this reading with the omitted element, is estimated as something like "your thought will be bewildered," or as "you see" functioning as the governing verb for *na'iman* ("bliss").

[Page 162]

It is said: ﴿عالِيَهم﴾ (ʿāliyahum) is a adverbial expression (ẓarf) meaning "above them," functioning as a predicate preceding its subject (khabar muqaddam, a predicate placed before its subject), while ﴿ثِيابُ﴾ (thiyāb, "garments") is a postponed subject (mubtadaʾ muʾakhkhar). The whole clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun attached to ﴿عالِيَهم﴾, so it explains the state of the righteous (al-abrār), who are the ones referred to by the pronoun.

Abū Ḥayyān said: ʿĀlī is itself a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from that pronoun, and it is an active participle (ism fāʿil), with ﴿ثِيابُ﴾ in the nominative as its agent (fāʿil). To establish that it is an adverbial expression (ẓarf), it would need to be transmitted from the speech of the Arabs, such as ʿāliyaka thawbun ("garment above you"), and similarly ʿāliyatan in the same sense. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of *laqqāhum* or from the pronoun of *jazāhum*, and it is said that it is from the implicit pronoun in ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾. All of these are remote. It is also permissible for the circumstantial clause to be from an omitted noun preceding ﴿نَعِيمًا﴾ or preceding (mulkan), meaning: "you saw people of bliss or people of dominion, above them etc.," but this is an artificial construction that is not needed.

It is also said: the circumstantial subject (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl) is the object pronoun in ﴿حَسِبْتَهُمْ﴾, so the clause explains the state of the attendants (al-ṭāʾifīn). Its remoteness is not hidden, because it entails a break in reference (tafkīk), since the pronoun in (saqāhum) afterwards seems clearly to refer back to the righteous, and a break in reference accompanied by a clear indicator is something that is not objectionable, yet this is disallowed.

It was also objected that the content of the clause becomes included under the supposing (al-ḥusbān), and how can that be, since they are actually wearing garments, unlike their being pearls, which is by way of comparison (tashbīh), requiring that their resemblance to pearls be close enough for them to be supposed pearls. It is answered that supposing in any state does not require that the state fall under the supposing, and ﴿خُضْرٌ﴾ is raised as an adjective (ṣifah) of ﴿ثِيابُ﴾ and ﴿إسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾ is raised as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on ﴿ثِيابُ﴾, meaning: "garments of brocade." Al-Sundus: Thaʿlab said: it is what is thin of brocade (dībāj). It is also said: what is thin of silk garments. The difference is that dībāj is a kind of woven silk that changes colors.

Al-Layth said: it is a kind of bazyūn (a type of thick cloth) made from al-marʿaz (soft wool). It is an arabized word (muʿarrab) with no disagreement among the lexicographers, according to al-Qāmūs and others. Some claimed that although it is arabized, its origin is *sindī*, with the relative *yāʾ* (yāʾ al-nisba), because it is imported from Sind, and the *yāʾ* was changed to *sīn*, as is said of sādiyy/sādis. But this is, as you see, unlikely. As for al-Istabraq: it is said to be what is thick of silk garments. Abū Isḥāq said: dībāj is the dense, thick, and fine kind. Ibn Durayd said: garments of silk similar to dībāj.

From Ibn ʿAbbād: it is a red cloak (burdah ḥamrāʾ). It is also said it is what is woven from gold. It is a non-Arabic term arabized, whose original in Persian is *istabarah*. In al-Qāmūs it is arabized from *istūrūh*, and this is reported from Ibn Durayd, who said it is Syriac. It is also said that it is arabized from *istafrah*, and the letter in the form of *fāʾ* is not a pure *fāʾ*, but is between *fāʾ* and *bāʾ*. It is also said that it is Arabic, and the Arabic language agrees with the language of others on it. al-Azharī approved this. Just as they differed over whether it is arabized or Arabic, they differed over whether it is an indefinite noun (nakira), or a generic proper name (ʿalam jins) that is indeclinable (mabnī), or arabized, or diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf), and whether its initial hamza is a hamzat qaṭʿ (cut hamza) or waṣl (linking hamza). The correct view, as al-Khafājī said, is that it is an indefinite noun, arabized, declinable (maṣrūf), with a cut hamza, as the recitation transmitted through multiple chains (al-qirāʾah al-mutawātirah) indicates. What contradicts it will be known, God willing. In Jāmiʿ al-Taʿrīb it is said that its plural is *abāriq* and its diminutive is *ubayraq*, the *sīn* and *tāʾ* being dropped in the broken plural because they were added together, so they are treated as a single addition. There is also disagreement on this matter, mentioned in its proper place. It did not mention the color of this istabraq. Nāṣir al-Dīn indicated that it is green, and so ﴿خُضْرٌ﴾ fits, and even if it is placed between the conjunct and the conjoined, it belongs to both. In any case, these garments are their clothing, and perhaps the verse implies that beneath them are other garments. It is also said, in the circumstantial sense from the pronoun in ﴿مُتَّكِئِينَ﴾, that the meaning is: above their canopies that are set up over them are garments of sundus, etc. The sum of this is that their canopies are adorned with sundus and istabraq.

Ibn ʿAbbās, according to one report from him, al-Aʿraj, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, Ibn Muḥaysin, Nāfiʿ, and Ḥamzah read ﴿عالِيهِمْ﴾ with a sukūn on the *yāʾ* and a kasrah on the *hāʾ*. This is the transmission of Abān from ʿĀṣim. Then it is nominative with a presumed ḍammah on the *yāʾ*, as a subject (mubtadaʾ), with *thiyāb* as its predicate (khabar). According to al-Akhfash, it is a subject (fāʿil) that takes the place of the predicate. It is also said that it is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam) and *thiyāb* is a postponed subject (mubtadaʾ muʾakhkhar), and it is taken as a predicate of an indefinite noun, since it is indefinite, and its genitive construction is verbal (iḍāfah lafẓiyyah), and it has the meaning of a group, as in ﴿سامِرًا تَهْجُرُونَ﴾ (al-Muʾminūn: 67), as Makkī explicitly stated. There is no need to commit to this according to al-Akhfash's view. It is also said that it remains in the accusative, with a presumed fatḥah on the *yāʾ*. You know that such a thing is anomalous or a poetic necessity, so the mutawātir recitation should not be interpreted in this way.

Ibn Masʿūd, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥah, and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ﴿عالِيَتُهُمْ﴾ with a *yāʾ*, and with the *tāʾ* damma. From al-Aʿmash also, and Abān from ʿĀṣim, the *tāʾ* is read with a fatḥah. Their grammatical analysis is like that of ﴿عالِيهُمْ﴾ with sukūn and naṣb.

Ibn Sīrīn, Mujāhid in one report, Qatādah, Abū Ḥayawah, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, al-Zaʿfarānī, and Abān also read ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ as a preposition with its object (jār wa majrūr), so it is a fronted predicate, and *thiyāb* is a postponed subject. ʿĀʾishah read ﴿عَلَتْهُمْ﴾ with a feminine *tāʾ*, as a past verb, with *fa-thiyāb* as its agent.

Ibn Abī ʿAblah and Abū Ḥayawah read ﴿ثِيابٌ سُنْدُسٌ﴾ with tanwīn on *thiyāb* and raising of *sundus*, as an attribute of it, as when we say "thawbun ḥarīrun," meaning "a garment of this kind of silk." The two Arab (Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī, or the two of Basra and Kufa, i.e., Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim?) — the text says al-ʿArabiyyān, meaning Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir? — and Nāfiʿ in one report read ﴿وَإِسْتِبْرَقٍ﴾ with a genitive, as a conjunction on *sundus*. Ibn Kathīr and Abū Bakr read ﴿خُضْرٍ﴾ with a genitive as an attribute of *sundus*, and it has the meaning of the plural.

They have explicitly stated that describing a collective noun, which is distinguished from its singular by the feminine *tāʾ*, with a plural is permissible and eloquent, and to this belongs ﴿وَيُنْشِئُ السَّحابَ الثِّقالَ﴾ (al-Raʿd: 12) and ﴿وَالنَّخْلَ باسِقاتٍ﴾ (Qāf: 10). The form *sundusah* has also come for the singular, as many have said. It is permissible that it is an attribute of *thiyāb*, with genitive by proximity (jarr al-jiwār), and in this there is agreement between the two readings in meaning, except that it is rare. Al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥah, al-Ḥasan, Abū ʿAmr according to one report from him, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿خُضْرٌ وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾ with genitive for both. Ibn Muḥaysin read ﴿وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾ with a connecting *alif* (waṣl) and a fatḥah on the *qāf*, as in most books of readings. From al-Kashshāf it is understood that he read it with a cut *alif* (qaṭʿ) and a fatḥah, and that others read as previously mentioned, which is contrary to what is known. The fatḥah reading was explained as being without tanwīn due to definiteness and foreignness, and it was criticized because it is an indefinite noun that can take the definite article, so one says *al-istabraq*. It is said that this is so-and-so. The connecting reading is based on the view that it is Arabic, a name derived from *istafʿala* from *al-barīq* (glitter). One says *barika* and *istabraqa*, like *ʿajiba* and *istaʿjaba*. So it is originally a past verb, then it was made a proper name for this type of garment, so it is diptote for definiteness and the verbal pattern, not for foreignness. It is objected that its being arabized is something that should not be denied.

It is also said that it is indeclinable, transferred from a clause of a verb and an implicit pronoun, and its state is not hidden. Abū Ḥayyān chose that *istabraq* in the reading of Ibn Muḥaysin is a past verb from *al-barīq*, as you have heard, and that it remains as such, not transferred, and not made a proper name for the known kind of garment. In it is a pronoun referring to the sundus or to the green (akhḍar) indicated by ﴿خُضْرٌ﴾, as if, when it was described as green, which in its intensity has darkness and dimness, he said that in that color there is a gleam and beauty that removes its dimness, so it was said ﴿وَإِسْتَبْرَقٌ﴾, meaning a flash and a shine, shining intensely. Then he said, alluding to those who made errors in it, such as Abū Ḥātim and al-Zamakhsharī, that this reading is better than condemning a noble, well-known reciter of mastery in Arabic, and charging with error a trustworthy authority who took from great scholars. End.

It is also said: the clause in this reading is parenthetical (muʿtaraḍah), or a circumstantial clause with *qad* assumed or without it. ﴿وَحُلُّوا أَسَاوِرَ﴾ is the plural of *siwār* (bracelet), which is well known. Al-Rāghib mentioned that it is arabized from *dastwārah*. ﴿مِن فِضَّةٍ﴾ means it is silver suitable for that abode. The apparent meaning is that this is a conjunction on ﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾. The difference between them in past and present tense is because the circumstantial sense precedes the renewed circulating. What is here is not contradicted by His words ﴿أَسَاوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ﴾ (al-Kahf: 31; al-Ḥajj: 23; Fāṭir: 33), since it is possible to combine them by multiplicity of bracelets for each person, alternation between wearing gold at one time and silver at another, and partition, such that some bracelets are gold and some are silver, due to differences in deeds.

It is also said: it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿عالِيَهُمْ﴾ with *qad* assumed or not. If the pronoun refers to the attendants, with ﴿عالِيَهُمْ﴾ as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *ḥasibtahum*, it is permissible to say that silver is for the servants and gold for those served.

It is permitted that the intended meaning of the bracelets is the lights overflowing upon the people of Paradise, varying according to variation in deeds, as gold and silver vary, and that the expression for them as bracelets of the hands is because they are the recompense for what their hands have done. It is not hidden that this is not suitable for exegesis, and it is more fitting to be of the category of allusion (ishārah). Then, if the adornment is for the youths (wildān), there is no issue, and they will be, on the second view, in ﴿مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾, "adorned with earrings" (muqarrarīn), and this is well placed in beauty. If the adornment is for the people of Paradise who are served, it is problematic, since it does not befit men but befits women and children. It is answered that this varies with differing customs and natures, and the creation of the Hereafter is other than this creation. Among the visible things in this world is that some of its kings adorn their upper arms, their crowns, and their chests with some kinds of jewelry, which for some temperaments are more suited to women and children, and they do not regard that as strange or deficient, all of which is due to familiarity and custom. So it is not far-fetched that among the natures of the people of Paradise in Paradise there is an inclination toward jewelry in general, especially since they are beardless, smooth, thirty years old.

It is also said that bracelets are only for the women of Paradise and children, but the masculine has prevailed in the wording, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

﴿وَسَقاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَراباً طَهُوراً﴾ — "And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink." This is another kind that surpasses the two preceding kinds, those mixed with camphor and those mixed with ginger, as indicated by the attribution of the giving of drink to the Lord of the worlds and the description of it as purifying. Abū Qilābah said: they are brought food and drink, and when that ends, they are brought the purifying drink, by which their hearts and bellies are purified, and sweat flows from their skins like the scent of musk. From Muqātil: it is water from a spring at the gate of Paradise, from the root of a tree; whoever drinks from it, God removes from his heart whatever deceit, rancor, and envy it had, and from his belly whatever filth and harm. If so, then *ṭahūr* in both is in the sense of *muṭahhir* (purifier). This has been discussed earlier, so recall it.

Many others said: the meaning is that it is at the utmost purity, because it is not filth like the wine of this world, which in the Sharīʿah is filth, since this abode is not a place of obligation; or because it was not pressed, so dirty hands do not touch it and dirty feet do not trample it, and it was not placed in jars and pitchers that have not been cleaned; or because it does not turn into impurity, since it is perspired as sweat from their bodies, with a scent like musk. It is also said: this drink is spiritual, not sensed, and it refers to the divine manifestation (tajallī rabbānī) that intoxicates them from everything other than Him:

*Clarity, with no water, subtlety, with no air, light, with no fire, spirit, with no body.*

Perhaps all that Ibn al-Fāriḍ mentioned in his Wine Ode (Khamriyyah), whose like was never poured into a cup, is an allusion to this drink, and it is what he meant by his words:

*They gave me to drink and said, "Do not sing," but even if they gave to drink the mountains of Ḥanīn, they would not have sung for me.*

It is related that Abu Yazid was asked about this verse, and he said: "He gave them to drink a drink by which He purified them from loving other than Him." Then he said: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted has a drink which He has stored up for the most excellent of His servants; He Himself undertakes to give it to them to drink. When they drink, they sway (ecstatically); when they sway, they fly; when they fly, they arrive; and when they arrive, they become united. They are ﴿in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]."

Some scholars interpreted all the drinks in a way other than their immediate sense. One of them said: The lights that overflow from the essences of the greatest angels and their chiefs, upon them be peace, upon these spirits, are likened to sweet water which removes thirst and strengthens the body. Just as springs differ in clarity, abundance and strength, so too the springs of the higher lights differ. Some of them are camphor-like, of the nature of cold and dryness, and the one who has them is, in this world, in a station of sorrow, weeping and constriction. Others are ginger-like, of the nature of heat and dryness, and their possessor pays little attention to the equable (temperate) and little regard to bodies and corporeal things. Then the human spirit continues to move from spring to spring and from light to light. There is no doubt that causes and effects are finite in their ascent toward the Necessary Existent, who is the Absolute Light, may His majesty be exalted. When it reaches that station and drinks that drink, those earlier drinks are digested, indeed they vanish, because the light of everything other than Allah is extinguished in the presence of the light of the majesty of Allah, glory be to Him, and His greatness. That is the final journey of the sincere (saddiqin) and the furthest point of their ascent and perfection. For this reason, Allah the Exalted concluded the mention of the reward of the righteous (abrar) with His words, majestic and exalted: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾.

﴿Indeed, this﴾, which He has mentioned of the various honors of exalted station, ﴿was a reward for you﴾, in return for your righteous deeds, which your good preparedness and your choice required. The apparent meaning is that the use of the verb ﴿was﴾ indicates certainty and permanence. It is also permissible that the meaning is: it was in My knowledge and My decree. The same applies to His words, exalted is He, ﴿and your striving was appreciated﴾, meaning: accepted and approved, or rewarded for, without being lost.

According to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, the speech is based on an ellipsis of the verb "say" (idmar al-qawl, the omission of a verb of saying understood from context), meaning: "And it will be said to them, after they have entered Paradise and witnessed what has been prepared for them: ﴿Indeed, this﴾ etc." The purpose is that their joy may increase, for it is said to the one who is punished: "This is because of your evil deed," so his grief increases, and to the one who is rewarded: "This is because of your obedience and your good deed," so his joy increases, and this is a congratulation to him.

It is also permissible that this is an address from God, exalted is He, in this world, as if He, glorified is He, after describing the reward of the people of Paradise, said: "Indeed, this was in My knowledge and My decree a reward for you, O assembly of My servants, and your striving was appreciated." It has been said: this does not dispense with the ellipsis, so that it may be connected to what precedes it. He, glorified is He, has mentioned of the reward that which moves the minds, and then followed it, exalted and high is He, with what indicates the good pleasure, which is the highest and most precious to the beloved:

If you are pleased with me, O desire of the heart,
I see everyone in existence smiling at me.

It is narrated through several chains that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited this surah when it had been revealed to him, and with him was a black man from Abyssinia. When he reached the description of the Gardens, the man sighed a sigh by which his soul departed. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Your companion's soul has departed out of longing for Paradise.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 23:

When the Exalted (subhanahu) first mentioned the condition of man, dividing him into the obedient and the disobedient, and elaborated, may His majesty be exalted, on what He has prepared for the obedient, pointing to the greatness of the vastness of His mercy, He mentioned what He honoured His Prophet (ﷺ) with, to remove his loneliness and strengthen his heart. So He, mighty in speech, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Qur'an to you, sending it down progressively﴾. That is, We sent it down in pieces, in stages, over about twenty-three years, for profound wisdoms that required it, not by anyone other than Us, as the repetition of the pronoun indicates, whether the separate pronoun is an emphatic (ta'kid), a separator (fasl), or a subject (mubtada'), for each of these is possible.

﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾: that is, in delaying your victory over the disbelievers, for its outcome is praiseworthy. ﴿And do not obey﴾ the lack of patience on your part with regard to their harm, and your impatience at the delay of your victory, ﴿any sinner or ungrateful one among them﴾. It has been said that "aw" (or) is for one of two things in all its uses, and other meanings occur to it, such as doubt, permission, and others. So the original meaning here is: ﴿do not obey from among them﴾ either of the two types. Since the most prevalent use of "aw" in a negative context is generality, and the possibility of anything else is a weak possibility, the meaning becomes a prohibition against obeying this one and that one. The conjunction "wa" (and) was not used, because the speech could be understood as a prohibition against the combination, and its compliance would be achieved by abstaining from one without the other. Thus it should not be objected that you should not obey one of the two types, since compliance is achieved by not obeying one of them without the other; for it is said of one who does that that he has not obeyed either of them. Hence it has been said that "aw" in an affirmative context indicates one of the two matters, while in a negative context it indicates the negation of both matters together. Perhaps what has been mentioned is the meaning of the words of Ibn al-Hajib (Ibn al-Hajib, the grammarian), where he said: the placement of "aw" is to establish the ruling for one of the two matters, except that if there is an indicator by which it is understood that one of the two matters does not prevent the other, such as your saying "sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," it is called permission; and if it prevents, then it is for one of the two matters. Some have objected to its occurrence in a prohibition, as in ﴿do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one﴾, since if one were to abstain from only one of them, he would not have complied.

For this reason, some, namely Abu 'Ubayda, took it to mean "wa" (and). The first view is that it remains in its proper function, and the generality in it came from elsewhere, namely the prohibition which carries the meaning of negation. This is because the meaning before the prohibition was: you obey a sinner or an ungrateful one, that is, one of them. When the prohibition came, it applied to what was already established in meaning, so the meaning becomes: do not obey one of them. Thus generality is brought into both from the side of the prohibition, while "aw" remains in its proper function, as mentioned, because abstaining from one of them is not achieved until one abstains from both. This differs from the affirmative, for one may do one of them without the other. End of quote.

Based on this, it has been said that the expression of generality in negation and in the prohibition that has its meaning is because the particular affirmative contradicts the universal negative. Close to this is the statement of al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) that "aw" here is more emphatic than "wa," because if you say, "Do not obey Zayd and 'Amr," and he obeys one of them, he is not disobedient; but if you replace it with "aw," it indicates that each of them is deserving of being disobeyed, and it is understood from it that the prohibition is against obeying both together, as is not hidden. Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) stated that "aw" remains in its literal meaning, and that the prohibition against obeying both of them came from the indication of the text, which is what is called the implicit meaning of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa) in its two divisions: the superior (al-awlawi) and the equal (al-musawi). So reflect.

The intended meaning of "the sinner" and "the ungrateful one" is their category. Linking the prohibition to these two qualities indicates that the two attributes are its cause. Therefore the prohibition against obedience must be in sin and disbelief, not in what is neither sin nor disbelief. The meaning is: do not obey one who commits sin and who invites you to it, or one who commits disbelief and who invites you to it. That is, do not follow any sinner when he invites you to sin, or any ungrateful one when he invites you to disbelief. For when it is said, "Do not obey the wrongdoer," it is understood that you should not follow him in wrongdoing when he invites you to it, and denying this understanding is obstinacy. Therefore the argument from the verse against the permissibility of following a deviant person when he leads prayer does not hold. Furthermore, the division is with regard to what they call to, namely disbelief and the sin opposite to it, not with regard to their persons, such that some of them would be sinners and some ungrateful, so it might be asked: how is that, when all of them are disbelievers? The intensification in "ungrateful" (kafur) has been said to be for conformity with reality. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ [Al 'Imran: 130]. Considering its return to the prohibition is like considering its return to negation, as has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], as you see.

It has also been said that the sinner is the hypocrite, and the ungrateful one is the open polytheist. It has been said that the sinner is 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, and the ungrateful one is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, because 'Utba was constantly engaged in sins and indulged in various kinds of wickedness, while al-Walid was extreme in disbelief and severe in obstinacy. It is narrated from Muqatil that they both said to him (ﷺ): "Turn back from this matter, and we will satisfy you with wealth and marriage," and so this was revealed.

It has been said that the ungrateful one is Abu Jahl, and the verse was revealed concerning him, but the earlier view is preferable. In the prohibition, despite his infallibility (ismah), there is guidance for one who is not infallible to humble himself before God, exalted is He, and to earnestly turn to Him, glorified is He, seeking protection from falling into what is not fitting.

And mention the name of your Lord ﴿in the morning and in the evening﴾. Persist in remembering Him, glorified is He, at all times. Or, persist in the prayers of dawn, noon and afternoon, since the evening (al-asil) may be applied to the period after the decline of the sun until sunset, so that it encompasses them both. ﴿And part of the night﴾, meaning some of it, ﴿prostrate yourself before Him﴾, that is, pray to Him, mighty and majestic is He. Here the prostration is a metonymy (majaz) for the prayer, by mentioning a part and intending the whole. Interpreting this as the prayers of maghrib and 'isha' is also possible, and the placing of the adverbial phrase first serves to show care and concern, because the night prayer involves greater effort and sincerity. ﴿And glorify Him through a long part of the night﴾, that is, perform tahajjud (night prayer) to Him, exalted is He, for a long portion of the night. This is a command to tahajjud, as some have chosen.

The tanwin (nunation) of ﴿layla﴾ indicates partitiveness (tab'id). The root meaning of tasbih (glorification) is declaring God free from imperfection, and it is applied to all acts of worship, both verbal and physical. It is reported from Ibn Zayd and others that this was obligatory and was abrogated (naskh), so that today there is no obligatory prayer except the five. Others said: it is muhkam (established, not abrogated) regarding the Prophet, peace be upon him. Still others said: it is likewise in general, in the manner of recommendation (nadb). It has been said that placing the adverbial phrase later indicates that it is not obligatory, like the preceding command, and likewise in expressing it by tasbih; but this is open to question. Al-Tibi said: The most appropriate reading in terms of the composition is that when God, exalted is He, forbade His beloved (ﷺ) from obeying the sinner and the disbeliever, and urged him to be patient in the face of their harm and their excessive enmity, and intended to guide him to disassociate from them, He followed that with a command to occupy all of his times with worship, by night and by day, through all the prayers without restriction, and with glorification as much as he is able, after the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾ ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and be among those who prostrate﴾ [al-Hijr: 97–98]. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, these﴾ — the disbelievers — ﴿love the immediate﴾ (al-'ajilah), and they immerse themselves in its perishable pleasures, ﴿and leave behind them﴾ — i.e., before them — ﴿a heavy day﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection. That it is "before them" is apparent; or the meaning is that they leave behind their backs a heavy day, not caring for it. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is said, on the first reading, to be a circumstantial clause (hal) modifying ﴿a day﴾; and on this reading it is the adverbial complement of ﴿leave behind﴾ (yadharun). If it is construed in one uniform manner regarding its dependence, it is also valid. Describing the day as "heavy" (thaqil) is to liken its severity to the weight of something harmful and burdensome to its bearer, by way of metaphor (isti'arah). The sentence serves as a reason (ta'lil) for what he was commanded and forbidden to do, as if it were said: "Do not obey them, and occupy yourself with the more important matter of worship, because these have abandoned the Hereafter for the sake of this world; so you leave the world and its people for the Hereafter." It has also been said that this conveys a warning (tarhib) to the lover of the immediate and an encouragement (targhib) to the lover of the deferred. The first is the cause for the prohibition against obeying the sinner and the ungrateful, and the second is the cause for the command to worship.

﴿We created them﴾, not anyone else. ﴿And We strengthened their joints﴾, meaning We firmly bound the joints with sinews and veins. The *asr* (binding, from the root meaning to tie or bind) originally means tightening and fastening, and the term is applied to that by which something is tightened and bound, as it is here. The intended meaning is the sinews and veins, because they resemble the ropes with which things are bound, and the aspect of resemblance is clear. From this, the *arif* (the gnostic, one who knows God through inner realization) may say: whoever's bond is from his own self, and whose prison is his worldly life, let him complain about the duration of his life and lament his very existence. The intended meaning of *asr* here is the strength of character and its being a good bond,

**Page 167 (continued)**

a good binding. From this comes the expression "a horse with a strong *ma'sur al-khuluq*" (a horse of firm disposition), when its binding is good. And it is reported from Mujahid that *al-asr* means *al-sharaj* (the anal passage), and he explained it as the passage through which waste leaves the body. Its being tightened means making it such that when filth comes out, it contracts.

It is not hidden that this falls within the strength of character and its being a good binding. ﴿And if We wish, We will replace their likes﴾, meaning We will destroy them and replace their likes in strength of character, ﴿a complete replacement﴾, a wondrous one without any doubt about it, meaning the resurrection and the second creation. Thus the replacement is in attributes, because the return is the origin of the beginning. Since the matter is certain and definitely going to happen, the conditional particle *idha* is used, and mentioning the will is to leave its timing vague. Similar usage is common, as a great person says to one who asks him for a favor: "If I wish, I will be kind to you."

It is also possible that the meaning is: "If We wish, We will destroy them and replace them with others who obey." In that case the replacement is in the essences, and *idha* (the conditional) indicates the certainty of His power over it and the certainty of what their disbelief requires, which is their annihilation. So He treats that power, which is threatened with, as if it were already realized, and expresses it in the way such a thing is expressed. This is probably what al-Zamakhshari intended by what is quoted from him: "It is only permissible because it is a warning given in the manner of emphasis, as if it had a specific appointed time." It cannot be objected to with the words of the Exalted, ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, not like you﴾ [Muhammad: 38], because rhetorical subtleties do not necessarily follow a consistent pattern. Understand this. The first interpretation is more fitting to the context of this sublime composition.

Indeed this is a reminder. ﴿Indeed this is a reminder﴾: a reference to the surah or to the Qur'anic verses.

﴿So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾: that is, whoever wills to take to Him, exalted is He, a way, meaning a means that conveys him to His reward. "He took it" means he drew near to Him through obedience. So the way is also a means to the goals.

﴿And you will not will﴾: that is, anything, or the taking of the way.

﴿Except that God wills﴾: that is, except at the time of God's willing, for your willing.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, ﴿And you will not will﴾ obedience ﴿except that God wills﴾, exalted is He, to compel you to it. This is a distortion of the verse without any evidence. According to what is in al-Intisaf, it would entail that the servant's will is not found except when it is negated, and this is far removed from the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that affirmed human free choice and divine justice), and is the furthest from it.

The apparent meaning is what we have established, because the omitted object is the one mentioned first, as you say: "If I had willed, I would have killed Zayd," meaning, "If I had willed the killing," not "If I had willed Zayd." The Mu'tazilah cannot dispute with the People of Truth (ahl al-haqq, the Sunni orthodox) on this, because willing is not among the voluntary acts; otherwise it would lead to an infinite regress. Rather, the act accompanying it proceeds from it. So the claim of the servant's full independence is arrogance, and likewise the claim of absolute compulsion (jabr) is a baseless claim. The matter lies between the two matters, to establish two wills. Its essence, as verified by al-Kawrani, is that the servant is free in his actions and not free in his choosing; reward and punishment are due to the goodness or evil of the innate disposition of the soul as it truly is (al-nafs al-amri). So each acts according to his own disposition. Glory be to Him who gave everything its creation and then guided it.

In al-Tafsir al-Kabir, this verse is among those verses in which the waves of qadar (divine decree and human agency) and jabr (compulsion) clash. The Qadariyyah (those who affirm human power over their acts) hold on to the first clause and say that its meaning is that the servant's will necessitates the act, and this is my doctrine. The Jabriyyah (those who deny human agency) hold on to the second clause and say that its meaning is that God's will necessitates the servant's will. From the two clauses it follows that God's will necessitates the servant's will, and the servant's will necessitates the servant's act, as the conditional form indicates. Therefore God's will necessitates the servant's act, because what necessitates a necessitated thing is itself necessitating, and that is compulsion. This is the clear doctrine of mine. It has been objected that this is not pure compulsion, in which choice is entirely negated, but rather it also returns to a matter between two matters. Some of the eminent scholars took the object of "yashā'" (wills) to be "the taking and the attainment," in order to answer the statement from its beginning. So he said: Indeed, His saying, glory be to Him,

**[Page 168]**

﴿And you do not will﴾, etc., is a confirmation of the truth, by clarifying that the mere will of people is not sufficient for taking the path, as is understood from the apparent meaning of the conditional sentence. That is, "and you do not will to take the path, nor are you able to attain it at any time, except at the time of His, the Exalted's, will to take it for you and to bring it about for you, since the will of the servant has no role except acquisition (kasb), while the causing and creating belong to the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." In this there is a kind of departure from the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

Yes, it has been said that the apparent meaning of the conditional sentence is that the will of the servant, unrestrictedly, necessitates the act, so that whenever he wills an act he would perform it, although the reality is otherwise. Therefore, what this party has said is necessary, and they made the second clause a confirmation of the truth. It has been answered that it is a confirmation in another manner: the first clause conveyed necessitation, and the second clause clarified that this necessitating will is not realized except at the time of Allah's, the Exalted's, will for it.

Thus it is as if it were said: "And you do not will a will that necessitates the act except at the time when Allah, the Exalted, wills your that will." So reflect.

You should know that this question is one of the things in which understandings are bewildered and feet slip, generation after generation. The strongest doubt of the Jabriyya (the determinist school) is that it has been established that a thing does not come into existence unless it is necessitated; so if the occurrence of the act is necessary, there is no choice; and if not, there is no occurrence. In other words: all that the act depends upon, when it is realized, either necessitates the act, and then compulsion follows; or it does not, and then it follows that the effect may be separated from its complete cause; and indeed, with occurrence, there is preponderance without a preponderant. It has been said that it is similar to the doubt of Ibn Kammuna on Divine Unity, from which escape is difficult.

For the poor and helpless one, may Allah, the Exalted, mend his poverty and ease his affair, he resolved to compose a treatise, if Allah the Exalted wills, on this matter, following in it, by His success, glorified is He, the best of paths. Although al-Kuwarani, may his secret be sanctified, left no room for speech in it, he was about to leave every one who comes after him in need of him for something in it. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Granter of success.

Al-Arabiyyan (Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿وما يَشاؤُونَ﴾ ("and they do not will") with the ya' of the third person. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿إلّا ما يَشاءُ اللهُ﴾ ("except what Allah wills"), in which ما is a verbal-masdar particle, like أنْ in the reading of the majority. We have already pointed out that the verbal noun (masdar) is in the position of an adverbial accusative (ẓarf), by estimating an omitted noun that stands in its place, and this is what many have chosen. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that they have stated that only an explicit verbal noun can stand in the place of an adverb (ẓarf), so it is not permissible to say أجِيئُكَ أنْ يَصِيحَ الدِّيكُ ("I come to you that the rooster crows") or ما يَصِيحُ الدِّيكُ ("what the rooster crows"); rather, it is permissible only to say أجِيئُكَ صِياحَ الدِّيكِ ("I come to you at the crowing of the rooster"). Perhaps for this reason it has been said that ﴿أنْ يَشاءَ﴾ ("that He wills") is, by estimating the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) and the exception, from the most evident of the causes; that is, ﴿وما تَشاءُونَ﴾ ("and you do not will") by a cause among the causes, except by that Allah the Exalted wills.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing﴾ — exceeding in knowledge, so He knows the wills of the servants that relate to the acts they asked for with the tongues of their preparedness (isti'dad). ﴿All-Wise﴾ — exceeding in wisdom, so He bestows upon each thing what is most suitable to its preparedness and to what it is in reality of will. Or, He, the Exalted, is exceeding in knowledge and wisdom, so He knows what each person deserves of obedience and its opposite, and therefore He wills for them only what His knowledge requires and His wisdom, Mighty and Majestic, demands. It has also been said: ﴿Knowing﴾ means He knows what the wills of the servants relate to of deeds; ﴿All-Wise﴾ means He wills only in accordance with His wisdom, which is that the servant wills and then the Lord, glorified and exalted, wills, not the reverse, so that obligation (taklif) may be realized without either of the two wills standing alone apart from the other. In this there is discussion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 76, verse 31:

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ etc. is an explanation of what the preceding sentence contained. It was said: that is, He, glorified is He, admits into His mercy whomever He wills to admit into it, and that is the one in whom He knows good, since He grants him success in what leads to entering Paradise, namely faith and obedience. ﴿And the wrongdoers﴾, that is, to their own detriment, are those in whom He knows evil, ﴿for them He has prepared a painful punishment﴾, extremely painful. The accusative of (the wrongdoers) is by an implied verb that is explained by "has prepared" etc. It was estimated as "He punishes," and it may be estimated as "He threatens," "He requites," or something similar. "Has prepared" was not estimated because it does not take a direct object with the preposition lam. Ibn al-Zubayr, Aban ibn Uthman and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "and the wrongdoers" (al-zalimun) in the nominative, as a beginning, but the reading of the majority is better.

Even if it necessitates an estimate for the antithesis (tibaq) in it, its departure in this [verse] is because the sentence there is nominal while the first is verbal. It cannot be said that emphasis is desired in the context of threat, because we say the matter is the reverse: if it were verified, wrath would precede mercy. Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read "and for the wrongdoers" (wa-li-l-zalimin) with the lam of genitive. It was said that it is connected to what follows for emphasis. It was also said that it is by estimating "He has prepared for the wrongdoers, He has prepared for them." The majority hold the first view. Furthermore, although this surah contains of the vastness of Allah's mercy what it contains, it has also pointed, through His great majesty, glorified and exalted is He, to what it has pointed to. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Majah, al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and others narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ until he finished it, then said: 'Indeed I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The sky has groaned, and it has the right to groan; there is not a space of four fingers in it but an angel is placing his forehead prostrating to Allah, the Exalted. By Allah, if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not enjoy women on beds, and you would go out to the high ground, crying out to Allah, the Exalted.'"

This seems to support what we have said. We ask Allah, the Exalted, to make us among the righteous, the near ones, the good, so that He grants us Paradise and silk, and makes our striving toward Him thankworthy, by the sanctity of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his purified family from uncleanness, with a thorough purification.
